World, giving children to the commonwealth, (Menochius) and employing themselves in useful arts. The Jews would not allow magicians, players, &c., to reside in their country. — Craft. They pray that they may succeed in their employment, while some also strive to comply with their religious duties. (Calmet) — Applying. Greek refers this to the following chapter, “As for him who applies his soul and meditates on the law of the Most High, he will,” &c. (Haydock)

Ancients. The Essenes (Josephus, Jewish Wars i. 7.) and Therapeuts (Philo, Comtemp.) were most famous for doing so. In general the Jews despise the learning of foreign nations: but some have applied themselves to it, particularly Philo, Josephus, &c., 1 Machabees i. 11., and 2 Machabees vi. 11.) — Prophets. These required the utmost study, before the coming of Christ, 1 Peter i. 11., and Daniel ix. 9. (Calmet) — The virtuous must follow both an active and contemplative life. (Worthington)

Sayings, or history of Abraham, &c. — Parables. This was most in vogue, 3 Kings x. — But mechanics abstained from this study, chap. xxxviii. 38. (Calmet) — To meditate well, 1. knowledge; 2. virtue; 3. humility; and 4. hope, are requisite. (Worthington)
Governor of the province or army. The most enlightened were chosen, like Joseph, Daniel i. 4., &c.
Men. Travelling was very requisite, (chap. xxxiv. 11.) and history records the actions of the bad as well as of the good, for the instruction of the public.
Pray. Diligence and prayer are the means to acquire wisdom, chap. iv. 13.
Lord, being in a sort of rapture, and enlightened by Him.
Generation. With what care do we not preserve the Scriptures? &c.
Thousand. Children or other men. — Rest, in death. (Calmet)
With. Greek, “as the moon in the first quarter,” dichomenia. The Vulgate has read Diomenia, “divine transport.” The author declares that he was inspired. (Calmet)
Voice. Greek, “songs of your lips, (Haydock) and with ancient lyres,” &c. (Calmet)
Waters. At the world’s creation, or at the passage of the Israelites. [Exodus xiv. 21., and Josue iii. 13.] (Calmet)
Salvation. None can prevent the salvation of God’s elect. (Haydock)
Wonderful, or new. (Calmet) — The greatest miracles cost him nothing. (Haydock)
Time. The veil shall be withdrawn, and Providence will appear. Greek, “all things are made for their proper use.”

That. Greek, “as he changed the waters into saltness,” (Haydock) at Sodom, (Calmet) “his ways are plain for the saints: so to sinners they are stumbling-blocks,” ver. 30. The Red Sea gave a passage to Israel, and overwhelmed the Egyptians. (Haydock) — Him. God does all with grandeur. He poured his graces upon Israel, and overwhelmed the giants in the deluge. (Calmet)
Good and, is omitted in Greek. Before the fall, all was happiness. Now, the wicked have still some mixture of good, ver. 32. (Bossuet)

Water and fire. These are requisite to prepare bread. The Romans refused them to the enemies of the state. — Cluster. Greek, “blood,” as [in] Deuteronomy xxxii. 14. (Calmet) — God gives the necessaries of life, which the virtuous use well, for their reward; and the wicked ill, to their ruin. (Worthington)
Evil. The good or bad use of them decides all, Wisdom xiv. 11., Romans viii. 18., and Titus i. 15.

Spirits. Storms (Psalm x. 7., and cxlviii. 8.) good angels, (Genesis xix. 11., and Isaias xxxvii. 36.) or rather devils: who, though created in holiness, fell, and became executioners of the wicked. (Calmet) — They abused their free-will, and are eternally punished. (Worthington)

Destruction, and final ruin of the impious, or at the last day. (Calmet) — Appease. God is pleased with the execution of justice. (Menochius) — Yet the devils cannot obtain a reconciliation; neither do they act to please God, having their wills obstinately bent against his, though they be forced to obey. (Haydock)
Beasts. Wolves, &c., with which the country was infested, Deuteronomy vii. 22., and xxii. 24. — Sword. War.
Feast. Greek, “rejoice,” as at a feast, Ezechiel xxxix. 16. — Word. They will be ready at the first sign. (Calmet) — All creatures, but the rebel angels and man, obey God. (Haydock)
Resolved. Literally, “confirmed” in this opinion by a divine light, ver. 16, 21.
Time. If we receive not at first, we must have patience.

That. Even sin contributes to manifest the justice and mercy of God; and we are not to judge of his works, but to praise him; as every thing is created for wise purposes, and evil proceeds from our abuse of things. (Calmet)

Labour, “anxiety,” ascholia. (Menochius) — All misery (Calmet) is in consequence of original sin. (Worthington) — The life of man is a trial, Job vii. 1., and xiv. 1. — Of all. The earth, (Calmet) which covers us, when all other things cast us away. (Pliny, [Natural History?] ii. 63.)
Purple. Literally, “hyacinth,” (Haydock) or violet colour. Purple was more like scarlet.
Knowledge. He is disquieted by restless (Calmet) and frightful dreams, ver. 6. (Haydock)
Fear, or no reason for it. (Calmet)
Beast. Their instinct causes them to fear death, to fight, &c.
Moreover. Greek, “death,” &c., are all destined for the wicked.
Out, and severely punished. (Calmet) — They shall not appear in the book of life.

Rejoice. The corrupt judge once rejoiced: but now he shall mourn. (Haydock) — The possessions and grandeur of the unjust shall end in a moment, like a clap of thunder, Psalm xxxvi. 36., and Proverbs x. 25. (Calmet)
And make. Greek, “they are unclean,” (Haydock) and will produce no fruit.

Weed. Literally, “verdure.” Greek Achei, (Haydock) properly denotes the rush, papyrus, which grows on the banks of the Nile, (Genesis xli. 2.; Calmet) and was used for fuel. (Alpin. i. 7.) (Matthew vi. 30.) — Thus the wicked will presently (Calmet) be treated. (Menochius)
Grace. The beneficent will produce fruits, like those of paradise, Genesis ii. 8.
That is. Greek, “and of one that.” — In it. Greek, “and more than both is one discovering a treasure,” (Haydock) who finds himself rich, without labour or injustice.
Both. Thus Judith, Zenobia, &c., ennobled their husbands, Proverbs xxxi. 10.
Wisdom. Virtue gives more content to the soul than corporal pleasures do to the body. It brings us near to God. (Calmet)
Green. “The sight of no colour is more agreeable to the eyes.” (Pliny xxxvii. 1.) — The Church is more excellent than the synagogue. (Worthington)
Husband. Their union is closer, and they can best assist each other.
Counsel. By this the Romans conquered the world, 1 Machabees viii. 31., and Proverbs xi. 14.
Heart, and make people presumptuous; while piety gives real courage, Psalm xxvi. 1. (Calmet)
It, or “him.” (Haydock) — The virtuous man is covered with glory.

Indigent. Greek, “live not by begging,” being too lazy to work, or incurring this punishment for thy sins, Leviticus xxvi. 16., Psalm cviii., and Deuteronomy xv. 4. Involuntary poverty is a most severe scourge. (Calmet) — All are bound to labour for what is needful; (Worthington) some by prayer, others by trade, &c. (Haydock)
Meat. Such is the condition of the parasite, (Calmet) and of the beggar. (Haydock)

Unwise. Some read, “impudent man,” with the Greek. — Fire. He shall feel the inconveniences of poverty; (Haydock) yet will not work, being lost to all shame. (Calmet) — Plato (Leg. 11.) orders magistrates to “clear the country of such an animal,” zoou, (Haydock) and the Lacedemonians suffered no beggars among them.
Death is terrible to all, but most to those who live comfortably. (Calmet) — O vita misero longa, felici brevis. (Seneca)
